title: Sh-M-A
hook: shema: hear, understand, obey, all at once

segments.voice: Yesterday, emet: alef, mem, tav, and the warning hidden in met. Your line was truth needs the one. Did you catch a true sentence missing its alef? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

"Did you hear me?" A parent in a kitchen asks it, and the kid nods. Yes. Ten minutes later the shoes are still in the hallway. So did they hear? Their ears did. In English we'd sort out what went wrong with three different verbs: they heard, but they didn't really listen, or they listened and didn't obey. Hebrew can do all of that with one root. Ten days ago you read it letter by letter, the first word of the Shema. Today we open what it means.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR ME?` → `HEARD, LISTENED, OBEYED.` → `ONE HEBREW ROOT.`

segments.voice: Sh-M-A. Shin, mem, ayin. Turn it four ways. First, hear. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The verse opens with a call to the ear: shema. Second, understand. In the Tower of Babel story, God confuses the builders' language, "that they may not understand one another's speech." The Hebrew verb behind understand there comes from this same root. The builders could still hear each other's voices. They just couldn't take in what was said. Third, obey. When Abraham is told that all the nations will be blessed through his descendants, the reason given is "because thou hast obeyed my voice." Obeyed, in Hebrew, is the same root again. Literally: you heard my voice. Fourth, Sinai. When the covenant is read to the people, they answer with two verbs: na'aseh v'nishma, we will do, and we will hear. Some teachers notice the order. Doing comes first, and hearing after, as if some things can only be understood by doing them. Put the four together and the Shema's first word asks for all of it at once: let it in, get it, and let it change what you do. In this root, hearing that changes nothing hasn't quite finished hearing.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `UNDERSTAND ONE ANOTHER'S SPEECH.` · `THOU HAST OBEYED MY VOICE.` · `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.` · then, large: `TO HEAR IS TO HEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen fully, once. Settle, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Start with the nearest sound: your own breath. Then widen. The room. Something humming. A car, a bird, a voice through a wall. Don't name them or judge them. Just let each one all the way in. When a thought starts to answer, or plan, or comment, notice it, and come back to the hearing. If you pray, you can say the first two words, Shema Yisrael, and then stop, and listen. The bell holds the time.
Sh-M-A. Shin, mem, ayin: to hear, to understand, to obey, all in one root. Today's word.
Your line: to hear is to heed. Today, in one conversation, listen all the way to the end before you answer, and then do the thing you were asked. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the evening and morning prayers and at bedtime, and it is customary to cover the eyes with the right hand while saying its first line.

match.prompt: one root, three meanings — tap the pairs.

myth: in Hebrew, hear and obey come from different roots
"thou hast obeyed my voice" uses the same root as shema: you heard my voice.
at Sinai, the people say "we will do" before "we will hear"
na'aseh v'nishma. some teachers make a lesson of the order.
they could still hear. the root says they could not understand.

fork.setup: the covenant has just been read aloud to the whole people at Sinai. you're in the crowd. what do they answer?
options: "we will hear it, and then decide."
"we will do, and we will hear."
fork.reveal: na'aseh v'nishma: doing comes first in their answer. some teachers read it as trust that understanding comes through doing.

original.note: Hebrew: he heard; the root shin, mem, ayin covers hearing, understanding and obeying.

trapdoor: what you thought: shema just means hear.
what it means: the same root means understand and obey, so hearing that changes nothing isn't finished.
what a scholar hears: Babel's builders 'could not understand' and Abraham 'obeyed', both with this root; Sinai's na'aseh v'nishma puts doing first.

Genesis 11:7 (yishme'u, understand) and Genesis 22:18 (shamata, obeyed) both use the root; confirm.
